title: Smoke in the Haze

pages.text:
*The Surveyor's Catechism, Thirteenth Saying: Do not assume that a blank on the map is a blank on the ground.*

The bearing was 214 degrees, and the haze was determined to make it 215. Isla walked with the compass held level at chest height, her eyes locked on the needle, while the world around her shifted in soft, grey waves. It was not fog, exactly. It was thicker, more deliberate, a suspension of dust and moisture that swallowed the horizon and erased the ground beneath their boots. She could not see the sky, so she could not see the stars, and for the first time in her life, Isla Corrin felt the specific, cold panic of a surveyor who has lost her reference point.

"Keep walking," she said, her voice sounding thin in the damp air. "Joss, watch the ground. Mags, keep the chain ready. Do not stop unless I stop."

Joss Harrowgate walked ahead of her, his tall frame hunched against the chill, his rust-red shirt dark with sweat and mist. He moved with the cautious, testing gait of a man who expected the earth to give way at any moment. Behind them, Mags Okoro hummed a low, tuneless melody, the iron cooking pot on her back clinking softly with her steps. The sound was the only thing in the world that felt solid.

They had been walking for two hours. The hilltops they had triangulated earlier were gone, dissolved into the grey soup. Isla checked the compass again. 214 degrees. She took another step. The ground under her boots changed from loose scree to packed earth, then to something softer, darker. Moss.

"There," Joss said, his voice tight with surprise.

Isla stopped. Through the swirling haze, a shape resolved itself. It was a bridge, low and arched, built of grey stone blocks that fitted together with a precision that spoke of skilled hands. It spanned a stream that was not on their chart. According to their survey, this stretch of the valley floor was a dry, sandy bed, part of the loose, drifting country. Yet here was water, clear and cold, rushing over smooth pebbles, and here was a bridge, mossy and ancient, spanning it with perfect, unbroken symmetry.

Isla stepped forward. The moss was thick and soft, smelling of rain and deep time. She reached out and touched the stone. It was cold, hard, and utterly still. It did not drift. It did not waver. It was fixed.

"Look at this," Mags whispered, dropping to her knees. She brushed away a layer of silt from the bank. "This is not loose land. This is old stone. And look at the water. It is flowing downhill. In this part of the valley, the water usually flows in circles."

Isla turned her head. The haze was parting, just slightly, revealing a slope rising gently to the left. And there, impossibly, against all logic and season, were trees. Not the scrubby, drifting bushes they had seen on the Marches, but tall, straight trees, their branches heavy with white blossoms. Apple blossoms. Out of season, in the middle of the Unmade, an orchard was in full, defiant bloom.
pages.image: A low, mossy stone bridge arches over a clear rushing stream in a misty valley, with a tall tree covered in white apple blossoms visible in the background through the haze.

pages.text:
The orchard stood as the first solid thing in the grey, a dense wall of white blossom and dark green leaf that seemed to push the haze aside like a hand parting a curtain. Isla stepped through the gap in the trees, her boots sinking into the rich, dark soil. The air here was different. Cooler, sharper, it smelled of apples and wet stone. It smelled like home, or at least like the memory of home, which was a dangerous thing to feel in the middle of nowhere.

Then she saw the roofs.

They were slate, dark and glistening, arranged in a neat, orderly row along the crest of the hill. Behind them, the mist thinned, and the shapes of houses emerged, small and sturdy, with smoke rising from their chimneys in steady, blue-grey columns. It was a village. A real, working village, complete with a mill. The mill wheel turned, slowly and steadily, driven by the same stream that ran beneath the bridge. The sound of the water was a constant, rhythmic hum, like the ticking of the great clock in the Guild hall, only softer.

Isla felt her breath catch in her throat. This was not a hallucination. This was not a trick of the haze. This was a community.

"Is that a bell tower?" Joss asked, his voice dropping to a whisper. He pointed to the structure at the center of the village, a square tower of grey stone that rose above the other buildings. It was modest, unadorned, but it was solid. It was fixed.

Isla nodded. She could not speak. Her mind raced, trying to reconcile what she saw with what she knew. The Atlas said this place did not exist. The Guild’s maps showed only blank space, a void of loose, drifting land. But here was stone, and wood, and water, and smoke. Here was life.

They moved forward, their footsteps crunching on the gravel path that led into the village. As they reached the center of the square, the playing children stopped. They stood in a group near the well, their faces pale and wary. They did not run. They did not scream. They simply watched, their eyes wide and dark, sizing up the three strangers with a silence that was more intimidating than any shout.

An old man stepped out from the shadow of the mill. He was tiny, wiry, with white whiskers and a patched green coat that looked like it had been repaired so many times it was more thread than fabric. He leaned on a stick, but he walked with a steady, deliberate pace. His eyes were sharp, clear, and they fixed on Isla with an intensity that felt physical.

He stopped in front of her. He did not bow. He did not smile. He simply looked at her, at her coat, at the brass pencils in her hair, and then he spoke. His voice was thin, but it was steady.

"Are you the Guild?"
pages.image: A tiny old man in a patched green coat leans on a stick, standing in a village square with slate-roofed houses and a mill in the background, looking up at Isla Corrin who stands in her mustard surveyor's coat.

pages.text:
Isla opened her mouth, but the words stuck in her throat. She glanced at Joss, then at Mags, but neither offered a rescue. She had to answer.

"Yes," she said. "We are."

The old man nodded, as if this were the most obvious thing in the world. "I am Perrin Ashdown," he said. "Elder of Ennis Vale."

He spoke the name with the gravity of a proper noun, a thing with weight and history. Isla felt a chill that had nothing to do with the temperature. Ennis Vale. She had seen that name in the Atlas, in the margin of a sheet marked "dissolved" in small, precise ink. It was not a place. It was a memory.

"You know this place?" she asked.

Perrin’s eyes narrowed. "We have lived here for four hundred years. My great-grandfather’s great-grandfather built the first house on this hill. We were here long before your Guild started drawing lines on paper."

Isla frowned. "But the maps..."

"The maps are wrong," Perrin said. It was not an accusation. It was a statement of fact, as neutral as saying the sky was blue. "Forty-four years ago, the roads vanished. One by one. The path to the Marches, the road to the ferry, the track to the mines. They just... went. The tax collector stopped coming. The post stopped. The markets closed. We were left off. Not by choice. By erasure."

He looked around the village, his gaze sweeping over the houses, the mill, the orchard. "We have held ourselves together by stubbornness. And by a very good mill. We grow what we can. We fix what breaks. We do not drift. We stay."

Isla looked at the mill wheel, which was turning steadily, and at the stone bridge, which was solid. They had not just survived the erasure; they had resisted it. They had held their shape in a world that wanted to dissolve them.

"How?" she whispered. "How do you keep it from drifting?"

Perrin smiled, a thin, tired expression. "We measure it ourselves. We check the walls. We check the foundations. We do not wait for the Guild to tell us where we are. We know. We have always known."

Isla felt a strange, hot sensation in her chest. It was anger, but it was also recognition. She was looking at a mirror of her own life. She, too, had been left off. She, too, had to hold her shape in a world that wanted to erase her.
pages.image: The old man Perrin Ashdown, tiny and wiry with white whiskers, stands in front of a slowly turning wooden mill wheel, looking at Isla Corrin with a serious, steady expression.

pages.text:
Isla pulled her notebook from her coat pocket, her fingers brushing the worn leather cover before she opened it. Her hand did not tremble, though the air in the square felt heavy and still, pressing against her like a held breath before a thunderstorm. She turned to the page where she had plotted the drifting hills, the hexagon of survey pegs, and the angles that bound them together in a geometric cage.

Her finger traced the lines, following the positions of the hills, the wandering stream, and the bridge they had sketched in haste. The ink was dry, the numbers precise, yet something about the arrangement felt incomplete, a triangle missing its third side.

"It is here," she said, her voice barely audible above the creak of the mill wheel. "The survey says it is here. Within a hundred yards of the old coordinates."

Perrin looked at her, his eyes sharp and unblinking. "The old coordinates?"

Isla looked up from the page. "The Atlas. The Guild’s Atlas. It lists this place as 'dissolved.' It says the land here is loose. It says the valley slid out of the map."

Perrin’s face hardened, the muscles in his jaw tightening beneath the skin. "It says we are not real."

"I think," Isla said, and the words came out clearer than she expected, striking the air with the precision of a plumb line finding true, "that it says the Guild made a mistake. And then they did not correct it. They just... left us off."

She thought of the benchmark in Vell, that hair’s width error that had thrown the whole city off, and how such a small discrepancy could unravel a kingdom. She thought of the Chancellor’s deadline, the fast sheet, the quick fixes, and the desperate desire to close the book and move on without checking the sum.

"You are one hundred and twelve people," she said. "You have been cut off from the kingdom. No tax, no post, no road. You are living in a gap in the map."

Joss stepped forward, his boots crunching on the gravel, his hands already moving as if he were measuring a beam. "Can you fix it?"

Isla looked at the village, at the stone, the wood, the water, and the people standing in the square, watching her with an intensity that felt like the focus of a lens. She thought of the land settling, the ripple of light, the long breath. She thought of her great-grandmother, Hester Corrin, whose name was on the old sheet, a name that had been treated as a cautionary tale rather than a truth.

"I don't know," Isla said. "But I think we can try."

She looked at Mags, then at Joss, waiting for the hesitation she did not see. "We need to measure this place. Properly. Not a fast sheet. A true survey. We need to find where it belongs."

Perrin looked at her for a long time, his gaze moving from her face to the notebook in her hand. Then he nodded, a single, decisive motion. "Then we will show you the way."
pages.image: Isla Corrin, in her mustard surveyor's coat, looks down at an open field-book with a map, while Perrin Ashdown stands behind her looking at the same page with a serious expression.

pages.text:
Perrin watched her with the same meticulous attention he might have given a new theodolite, his gaze tracing the brass sighting-compass on the cord at her neck, the two crossed pencils holding her auburn knot, and the ink-stained fingers that gripped the notebook. He was cataloguing her parts, checking them for wear and function, and Isla felt the familiar prick of exposure that came from being looked at without any of her usual deflections or jokes.

"You are of the Guild," he said. It was not a question. It was a statement of fact, delivered with the calm certainty of a man who had spent forty-four years watching the world arrive exactly as he had predicted it would.

"Yes," Isla replied.

He was quiet for a moment, his eyes drifting to the orchard behind her. The wind shifted, and the blossoms on the apple trees rustled, releasing a faint, sweet scent that cut through the smell of the mill dust. The children in the square were still watching, but their shoulders had dropped, their curiosity now outweighing their fear.

"What is your name?" Perrin asked.

Isla hesitated. She had not thought about her name in a long time. In the Guild, it was just a label, a thing that closed doors rather than opening them, a reminder of the scholarship she had scraped by on and the family she was supposed to be ashamed of.

"Isla," she said. "Isla Corrin."

The old man went very still. The stick in his hand stopped its gentle tapping against the cobblestones. The silence that followed was not empty; it was full, heavy with a history that Isla did not fully understand but could feel pressing against her eardrums.

Perrin’s eyes widened. He looked at her, really looked at her, and for the first time, the hardness in his face softened. He smiled, slowly, and the smile reached his eyes, crinkling the skin around them.

"Hester’s child," he said. His voice was soft, almost a whisper, but it carried clearly in the quiet square. "Are you?"

Isla did not answer. She did not have to. The name hung in the air, a tenuous thread connecting the erased to the found, the past to the present.

"We wondered when someone would come back," Perrin said.
pages.image: The old man Perrin Ashdown, tiny and wiry, smiles warmly at Isla Corrin, who stands in her mustard surveyor's coat with two brass pencils in her hair, looking surprised and touched.
